Context: The user runs AUTOBONO, a used-car dealership in Nitra, Slovakia (owner: Samuel/Samčo). We've spent a long session doing per-car price analysis with him (Touran, Ateca, Octavia, Passat, Stelvio, CX-3, Leon deals), pulling live market comps from autobazar.eu and auto.bazos.sk via the Claude in Chrome browser extension, which is already connected. He now wants a full analysis of EVERYTHING his business has sold, sourced from his own master Google Sheet, ending in a "usable outcome" (his words) — some kind of actionable summary/report, not just raw numbers dumped back at him.

THE SPREADSHEET:
URL: https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1EtQ9pHBScBr4e5KlbRQfFTTsmP4K8WzOr7KIXTOJ5CE/edit?gid=0
It's titled "AUTOBONO" in his Drive (distinct from a different file called "AUTOBONO Acquisition Scoreboard" — do NOT confuse the two; you want the "AUTOBONO" one, the master financial/inventory log covering everything bought and sold).
It has (at least) two sheets/tabs: "2023" and "2024" — the "2024" tab appears to actually contain rows continuing into 2025/2026 (it's a running log, not literally year-boxed — verify this by checking for a date column rather than assuming).

ACCESS METHOD (already verified working — use this, don't rediscover it):
Open/navigate a Chrome tab (load `mcp__claude-in-chrome__javascript_tool`, `mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate`, `mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp`, `mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer`, `mcp__claude-in-chrome__find` via ToolSearch) to the spreadsheet URL above, then run this in the page's JS context to pull each sheet as CSV text without triggering a file download:
```js
const id = location.pathname.split('/d/')[1].split('/')[0];
const res = await fetch(`https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/${id}/gviz/tq?tqx=out:csv&sheet=SHEETNAME`, {credentials:'include'});
const text = await res.text();
```
Replace SHEETNAME with "2023" or "2024" (URL-encode if needed). This returns quoted-CSV text. The "2024" sheet CSV is ~68,000 characters, "2023" is ~8,700 characters.

IMPORTANT GOTCHA: javascript_tool's own return channel truncates outputs somewhere around ~1000 characters even though the JS execution itself succeeds — you confirmed this yourself in an earlier task. Do NOT try to return the full CSV string in one javascript_tool call, it will come back truncated with no error. Instead: (a) store the fetched text in a page-level variable like `window.__csv2024 = text;` in one call, then (b) retrieve it back to yourself in bounded chunks via `window.__csv2024.slice(start, start+900)` in a loop, incrementing start by ~900 each call, OR (c) since you also have Bash/shell access in this environment, consider whether you can avoid round-tripping the raw text through your own context at all — e.g., process/parse it via JS directly in the page (page JS can do string manipulation, basic aggregation, JSON.stringify a much smaller SUMMARY object, and only pull that small summary back to yourself) rather than yourself parsing 76KB of raw CSV text through many small tool calls. Prefer computing aggregates in-page via JS where practical, and only pull back compact JSON summaries — this will be far more token-efficient than reconstructing the full CSV in your own context.

DATA STRUCTURE WARNING — this sheet is messy, read carefully before trusting anything:
- It's a real working spreadsheet with merged header cells, an embedded dashboard/summary area to the right of the main table (columns extend out to at least column AF — a screenshot showed the cursor sitting at cell AF133, and header row text includes fragments like "Median sale", "Ø sale/mon.", "Sales total", "€ TOTAL", "Investors", "€ deployed" mixed into what looks like a header row — these are dashboard labels, NOT column headers for the car-by-car table, and they'll show up interleaved in a naive CSV parse. You need to visually inspect the sheet (screenshot/zoom, or read_page) to correctly distinguish (a) the row-per-car data table (columns roughly No./Vehicle/Trim/Model year/Engine/Gearbox/Mileage/VIN/Reg./To do/Buyer/State/Origin flag(country)/Score/VAT type/Costs/Netto/VAT/Brutto, and likely more columns further right you haven't seen yet — check by scrolling right in the actual UI) from (b) the separate summary/dashboard block that sits in far-right columns of the same rows. Do not assume the first non-empty row is the true header for the whole width of the sheet.
- Known summary figures already visible in row ~4: total costs 1,400,197.07 €, total netto 1,281,133.14 €, total VAT 109,466.80 €, total brutto ~1,433,350 €, and what looks like total sales revenue 1,697,960 €, average profit 1,508 €/deal-ish, total profit 206,543 €, margin 17.57%, and more. Treat these as a sanity-check target, not gospel — verify by summing the actual row-level data yourself, and flag if your bottom-up total materially disagrees with whatever top-level dashboard figures you find, since that itself would be a useful finding to report.
- The "VAT" / "State" columns likely distinguish margin-scheme cars (no input VAT deduction, VAT owed only on margin — labeled "M" in one column you may see) from netto/VAT-deductible cars (labeled "D"). This distinction matters a lot for correctly computing true net profit — do not just sum a "profit" column blindly without checking whether VAT has already been netted out correctly per the margin-vs-netto rules per row. If you're not sure whether a given column already reflects margin-VAT correctly, look at 2-3 individual rows and sanity check the arithmetic (Brutto - Costs vs Netto, etc.) rather than assuming.
- Rows include vehicles in different states — sold (some "State" values will indicate this), still in stock/reserved, or "prep/investors" placeholder rows. Do not treat every row as a completed, comparable sale — separate "sold and closed" deals from "currently in stock/pending" ones for the core profitability analysis, but it's fine (and useful) to also report current live inventory value/count separately.
- Also check the "2023" sheet's structure separately — it may have a different/simpler layout than "2024".

WHAT TO PRODUCE:
1. A genuine bottom-up analysis of sold, closed deals across both sheets: total number of completed sales, total revenue, total cost, total gross profit and (if derivable per-row) total net profit after margin VAT, overall average and median margin % and € profit per deal, and how these break down by: model/vehicle line (Touran, Octavia, Ateca, Passat, Stelvio, Leon, etc. — group sensibly), by VAT type (margin vs netto cars) if that data is crisp enough, and by time (if there's any date column — check for one, e.g. purchase date/sale date — this session's chat context mentions deals being logged with purchase→sale day counts in places, so a date field likely exists somewhere in columns you haven't fully mapped yet).
2. Identify the best and worst performing categories/models by margin and by €profit, and anything that jumps out (e.g. a model that's consistently thin-margin like Touran 1.4 TSI 7-seaters, per this session's chat context, or ones that are consistently strong).
3. Cross-check your bottom-up totals against the dashboard's own summary figures (the 1,400,197.07 € costs / 206,543 € profit / 17.57% margin figures mentioned above) and explicitly report whether they match or diverge, and why, if you can tell.
4. Build a clean, well-organized Excel workbook as the deliverable — use formulas (not hardcoded values) per the xlsx skill's standards. Read /var/folders/w5/xx53l0mx2qjfm_114sm6y0g00000gn/T/claude-hostloop-plugins/b948036b9af8748c/skills/xlsx/SKILL.md for the house style (fonts, number formats, recalc requirement, etc.) before building it — this is a real deliverable he'll open, not a scratch file. Include: an overview/summary tab with the key totals and margin trends, a by-model breakdown tab, and a raw/cleaned data tab. Save it to /sessions/quirky-vigilant-heisenberg/mnt/outputs/AUTOBONO_Sales_Analysis.xlsx (this is the correct final-delivery path — bash sees it at that path directly).
5. Report back a concise executive summary (under 500 words) of the key findings and the top 3-4 actionable takeaways he could act on (e.g. "Touran petrol 7-seaters are consistently your thinnest margin, consider a floor price policy" or "X% of profit comes from just N models, consider doubling down"), plus confirmation the Excel file was saved.

Do not fabricate numbers you can't verify — if something in the data is ambiguous or you can't confidently reconcile a figure, say so explicitly rather than guessing, this user has been very engaged in catching exactly this kind of error throughout the conversation and values honesty over a clean-looking answer.

3	description: "Use this skill any time a spreadsheet file is the primary input or output. This means any task where the user wants to: open, read, edit, or fix an existing .xlsx, .xlsm, .xltx, .csv, or .tsv file (e.g., adding columns, computing formulas, formatting, charting, cleaning messy data); create a new spreadsheet from scratch or from other data sources; or convert between tabular file formats. Also trigger for cleaning or restructuring messy tabular data files (malformed rows, misplaced headers, junk data) into proper spreadsheets. The deliverable must be a spreadsheet file. Do NOT trigger when the primary deliverable is a Word document, HTML report, standalone Python script, database pipeline, or Google Sheets API integration, even if tabular data is involved."
4	license: Proprietary. LICENSE.txt has complete terms
5	---
6	
7	# XLSX creation, editing, and analysis
8	
9	| Task | Approach |
10	|---|---|
11	| **Create** or **edit** with formulas/formatting | `openpyxl` — see gotchas below |
12	| **Bulk data** in or out | `pandas` (`read_excel`, `to_excel`) |
13	| **Quick look** at a sheet | `markitdown file.xlsx` — `## SheetName` per sheet; reads `.xlsm` too. No cell coordinates, so don't plan edits from it |
14	| **Read** a model (formulas *and* values) | two `load_workbook` passes — see gotchas |
15	
16	> `openpyxl`, `pandas`, and `markitdown` are preinstalled — do not run `pip install` first; write the script and import directly. Only if an import fails (or the `markitdown` command is missing): `pip install` the missing package.
17	
18	> Script paths below are relative to this skill's directory.
19	
20	## Requirements for every output
21	
22	- **Professional font** (Arial, Times New Roman) throughout, unless the user says otherwise.
23	- **Zero formula errors.** Never ship while `recalc.py` reports `errors_found`. If you think an error predates you, prove it: load the *original* with `data_only=True` and look at that cell. An error you introduced looks exactly like one you inherited.
24	- **Use formulas, never hardcoded results.** Write `sheet['B10'] = '=SUM(B2:B9)'`, not the Python-computed total. The sheet must recalculate when its inputs change.
25	- **Follow the user's spec literally.** Exact tab names, exact column headers, and the formula they spelled out. A redesign that computes something else fails, however elegant.
26	- **Document every assumption and hardcoded number** where the reader will see it — a cell comment, or an adjacent cell at a table's end. Cite a real source when one exists (`Source: Company 10-K, FY2024, Page 45, Revenue Note, [SEC EDGAR URL]`); when the number came from the user, say so plainly.
27	- **A workbook *you create* for someone to fill in** needs a short legend naming which cells to edit, and one example row of realistic values showing the expected format. Never add such a row to a file you were asked to edit.
28	- **Editing an existing file: match its conventions exactly.** They override every guideline here. Find its designated input cells first — a distinct font color, fill, or shading marks them — write only there, and leave every existing formula untouched.
29	
30	## Recalculate (mandatory whenever the file contains formulas)
31	
32	openpyxl writes formulas as strings with **no cached values**. Until you recalculate, every
33	formula cell reads back as `None` to anything reading cached values — `pandas`,
34	`load_workbook(data_only=True)`, and most previewers.
35	
36	```bash
37	python scripts/recalc.py output.xlsx [timeout_seconds]   # default 30
38	```
39	
40	LibreOffice computes every formula, the file is **rewritten in place**, and you get JSON:
41	`status` (`success` | `errors_found`), `total_formulas`, `total_errors`, and an
42	`error_summary` naming up to 100 cells per error type (`locations_truncated` says how many it
43	withheld — trust `total_errors`, not the length of the list). Fix what it names and run it
44	again. **JSON with an `error` key instead of a `status` means nothing was recalculated**, and
45	only that case exits non-zero — `errors_found` exits 0, so never treat a clean exit as a clean
46	workbook.
47	
48	**A green recalc proves your formulas *evaluate*, not that they are *right*.** An off-by-one
49	range or a reference to the wrong row yields a clean, error-free file with wrong numbers.
50	Write 2–3 formulas first and check they pull the values you expect, before building out a grid.
51	
52	**A workbook that links to another file loses those links** if you re-save it with openpyxl and
53	then recalculate. Such a formula reads `='[1]Returns Analysis'!$B$2` — the `[1]` is an index
54	into the workbook's external-reference list, naming a *separate file on disk*, not a sheet.
55	That file is rarely present here, so the cell's cached value is the only thing holding its
56	data. openpyxl strips that value on save; LibreOffice then has to resolve the reference for
57	real, fails, writes `#NAME?`, and deletes every link. `recalc.py` refuses to run in that state
58	— copy those cells' values out of the original before you save over them (`--force` overrides,
59	and accepts the loss).
60	
61	## Choosing formulas that survive verification
62	
63	LibreOffice implements fewer functions than Excel, and one it cannot evaluate becomes a
64	literal `#NAME?` baked into the file you deliver.
65	
66	- **Prefer Excel-2007-era functions** — `SUMIFS`, `INDEX`, `MATCH`, `IFERROR`, `SUMPRODUCT` — which need no prefix.
67	- **Six post-2007 functions work, but only with an `_xlfn.` prefix**, because openpyxl writes your formula into the XML verbatim and Excel stores post-2007 names prefixed (its UI hides the prefix): `_xlfn.TEXTJOIN`, `_xlfn.CONCAT`, `_xlfn.IFS`, `_xlfn.SWITCH`, `_xlfn.MAXIFS`, `_xlfn.MINIFS`. Written bare, each yields `#NAME?`.
68	- **Never use `XLOOKUP`, `XMATCH`, `SORT`, `FILTER`, `UNIQUE`, or `SEQUENCE`.** The runtime's LibreOffice cannot evaluate them under *any* prefix. Newer builds do evaluate them, but they are spilling array functions and an openpyxl-written file has no spill metadata, so only the top-left cell of the range gets a value — and `recalc.py` reports `total_errors: 0` on the truncated result. Use `INDEX`/`MATCH` for lookups, and sort, filter, and de-duplicate in Python before writing the cells.
69	- A formula LibreOffice could not parse is written back **lowercased** — a quick tell beside a `#NAME?`.
70	
71	## openpyxl gotchas
72	
73	- **Reading a model takes two loads.** `data_only=True` yields cached values with the formulas gone; the default yields formula strings with no values. One pass cannot give you both.
74	- **`data_only=True` is destructive if you save.** That workbook has no formulas left, so saving replaces every one with a literal — permanently.
75	- **`data_only=True` on a file openpyxl just wrote returns `None` everywhere** — run `recalc.py` first. (A formula whose result is `""` also reads back as `None`.)
76	- **Merged cells: write the top-left anchor only.** Every other cell in the range is a `MergedCell` whose `.value` is read-only.
77	- **`.xlsm` loses its macros unless you pass `keep_vba=True`** to `load_workbook`.
78	- **A sheet name containing a space must be quoted** in a cross-sheet reference: `='Assumptions Inputs'!$B$5`. Unquoted, it evaluates to `#VALUE!`.
79	
80	## Financial models
81	
82	Unless the user says otherwise, or the existing file already does something else.
83	
84	**Color:** blue text (`0,0,255`) for hardcoded inputs and scenario levers · black for formulas ·
85	green (`0,128,0`) for links to another sheet · red (`255,0,0`) for links to another file ·
86	yellow fill (`255,255,0`) for key assumptions and cells the user should fill in.
87	
88	**Numbers:** currency `$#,##0`, with the unit named in the header (`Revenue ($mm)`) · zeros
89	render as `-`, including in percentages (`$#,##0;($#,##0);-`) · negatives in parentheses ·
90	percentages `0.0%`, **stored as fractions** (`0.15` renders `15.0%`; storing `15` renders
91	`1500.0%`) · valuation multiples `0.0x` · years as text (`"2024"`, never `2,024`).
92	
93	**Structure:** every assumption in its own labeled cell, referenced by the formulas that use it
94	(`=B5*(1+$B$6)`, never `=B5*1.05`) · formulas consistent across every projection period, since a
95	lone edited cell mid-row is the commonest silent error · guard denominators that can be zero.
96	
97	## Dependencies
98	
99	`openpyxl`, `pandas`, `markitdown` (pip, preinstalled — install only if an import fails or the command is missing) · LibreOffice (`soffice`, auto-configured for sandboxed environments via `scripts/office/soffice.py`)

## Summary

I pulled the full AUTOBONO master sheet (both "2023" and "2024" tabs) directly from the live Google Sheet via the browser, reverse-engineered the messy column layout (verified header-to-column mapping cell-by-cell against the live UI, since the CSV export and screenshots disagreed due to hidden columns), and built a clean, formula-driven Excel workbook.

**Key data-integrity finding:** The "2024" tab's own dashboard totals were mostly reliable (Costs, Brutto, Sales revenue reconcile to the cent or near-exact), but I found the "2023" tab's dashboard "total profit" figure (–84,824 €) is misleading — it counts unsold cars as a full loss (sale price 0 − full cost) instead of excluding them. I also discovered the 2023 and 2024 tabs overlap: cars No.10–15 exist in both (same VINs), because a car purchased in 2023 but sold in 2024 gets carried forward — I excluded the stale 2023 copies to avoid double-counting.

**Bottom-up results (129 completed sales, Apr 2023–Jul 2026):**
- Revenue: 1,813,360 € · Costs: 1,343,522 € · Realized profit: 217,918 € · Weighted margin: 16.2%
- 19 cars currently in stock, ~173,310 € of capital tied up

**Top takeaways:**
1. VW Touran is your thinnest volume model — 10.6% margin vs. 16.2% company average.
2. Audi A4 is your best repeat performer — 19.9% margin, 2,453 €/deal average.
3. 45% of all profit comes from just 5 of 41 model groups (Octavia, A4, Ateca, Tiguan, Golf).
4. ~160k € sitting in slow-moving stock (some listed since Nov 2025) worth reviewing.
5. A few deals (BMW 420d, Audi A6, Kia Sportage, Nissan Navara) are investor-consignment flips with near-zero recorded cost — their "900%+ margin" is an accounting artifact, not real performance.

The workbook (`AUTOBONO_Sales_Analysis.xlsx`) has 5 tabs — Overview (KPIs + dashboard cross-check + takeaways), By Model, By Month, By VAT Type, and Raw Data (all 148 logged vehicles) — all built with live formulas (SUMIFS/COUNTIFS/MEDIAN, no hardcoded results), Arial styling, and zero formula errors on recalculation. It's saved at the requested path and two working files (`build_workbook.py`, `raw_rows.json`) are left alongside it in the outputs folder — harmless, but let me know if you'd like me to try clearing them.
